steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual overview of a Transformer neural network

1. Goal  
   A Transformer is designed to model relationships inside a sequence—words in a sentence, frames in a video, tokens in code—so it can produce another sequence (translation, summary, answers) or a representation useful for downstream tasks.

2. Fundamental idea: “Pay selective attention”  
   Instead of processing tokens strictly left-to-right (RNNs) or scanning with fixed-size windows (CNNs), a Transformer lets every token look at, and hence interact with, every other token in the sequence. It decides how strongly to “pay attention” to each other token through learned weights. This attention is calculated in parallel for all tokens, allowing both global context and computational efficiency on modern hardware.

3. Building blocks  

   a. Token embeddings  
      Each discrete symbol (word-piece, byte, etc.) is mapped to a continuous vector. A positional encoding (learned or sinusoidal) is added so the model knows order, because pure attention is permutation-invariant.

   b. Multi-Head Self-Attention  
      • Self-attention: For one layer, every token i creates three learned projections:  
        – Query vector qᵢ  
        – Key vector kᵢ  
        – Value vector vᵢ  
        Attention score from token i to j is qᵢ · kⱼ / √d. After softmax, these scores weight the value vectors vⱼ, producing a context vector for i.  
      • Multi-head: The above is repeated H times with different learned projections. Each “head” focuses on different relational aspects (syntax, long-range coreference, etc.). Outputs are concatenated and linearly mixed.

   c. Feed-Forward Network (FFN)  
      After attention, each token’s vector is passed through the same position-wise two-layer MLP (usually with ReLU/GELU) to mix features non-linearly.

   d. Add & Norm  
      Each sub-block (attention or FFN) is wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization:  
      output = LayerNorm(x + SubLayer(x))  
      This stabilizes training and eases gradient flow.

4. Encoder vs. Decoder  

   Encoder (BERT, ViT, etc.)  
   • Stack N identical layers of the components above.  
   • Pure self-attention sees all tokens bidirectionally.  
   • Final hidden states are contextualized representations.

   Decoder (GPT, language generation)  
   • Also stacked, but attention is masked so token i can only see tokens ≤ i—ensuring autoregressive generation.  
   • Often includes an extra encoder-decoder attention to read the encoder’s outputs (in translation).

5. Training objectives  

   • Autoregressive language modeling: predict next token given previous (GPT).  
   • Denoising / masked language modeling: guess masked tokens (BERT).  
   • Sequence-to-sequence supervised loss: match ground-truth translation, summary, etc.  
   • Many other tasks can be cast as token classification or span extraction.

6. Why it works  

   • Global receptive field: Direct paths between any two tokens make long-range dependencies easy.  
   • Parallelism: All positions processed simultaneously—well-suited to GPUs/TPUs.  
   • Expressivity: Multi-head attention can learn diverse relational patterns.  
   • Depth: Stacking layers composes increasingly abstract representations.

7. Computational view  

   For sequence length L and hidden size d:  
   • Self-attention cost: O(L² d) (quadratic in length). Work on “efficient Transformers” aims at sub-quadratic approximations for very long inputs.  
   • FFN cost: O(L d²).  
   • Memory likewise scales quadratically in vanilla attention.

8. Intuitions & analogies  

   • Each layer = a set of “soft hash tables”: queries seek matching keys; values deliver information.  
   • Multi-head = looking through different “relation lenses” simultaneously.  
   • Residual stacking = iterative refinement; later layers correct or enrich earlier hypotheses.

9. From components to behavior  

   During training, gradients push the attention matrices and FFN weights so that causal chains (e.g., “dog → it” coreference) have high attention, enabling correct predictions. Emergent properties such as syntax, world knowledge, and reasoning stem from layers composing these learned relations.

10. Practical variants  

   • ALBERT compresses weights; RoBERTa tweaks training; T5 unifies tasks.  
   • Vision Transformers adapt patches of an image as tokens.  
   • Performer, Longformer, etc. reduce attention cost.  
   • Mixture-of-Experts splits feed-forwards among specialist subnetworks for scale efficiency.

In essence, a Transformer is a stack of modules that repeatedly re-weigh inter-token relationships (self-attention) and transform those weighted mixtures (feed-forward), all while preserving information with residuals. This combination allows it to learn powerful sequence representations and generate coherent outputs across many domains.
